# The Commerce deck

**What it rewards:** Wealth from connection. Trade routes, trading posts, partnerships, resource wealth and deliberate spending. The deck is weak at production; it buys what other empires build and turns gold into production. **Directions inside it:** mining districts and mineral exports; luxury stockpiles and monopolies; domestic provisioning; overseas posts and exploration; reserves versus purchased capability.

*Initially generated by `scripts/deckDocs.mjs`; now a hand-edited design spec (deck-list pass, 2026-10-06). **Built** means the effect exists in the game, **revised** means this sheet changes a live effect, **new** means a card proposed in the deck-list pass of 2026-10-06 (its last column says whether existing effects can express it or what it needs), and **deferred** means the proposed effect is not implemented. Government tiers here are proposed availability, not confirmation of runtime unlocks. The generator runs only on request and overwrites these edits.*

**Review (2026-10-06).** Target: about 45 to 55 exclusive cards, shaped roughly 9 / 14 / 14 / 10 / 3. Before: 93. After: 47 (7 / 13 / 14 / 9 / 4). The reconciliation of the six sheets (2026-10-06) cut The Treasury Guard and The Condottieri in favour of Dominion's War Bonds and Mercenary Contracts, which are now shared with this deck, and restored The Chartered Company and Books from the Ships as shared cards. Every deferred card was cut. What stays is built, or new and either fits existing effects or waits on commissions or one small new reading. Tier 0 sits under its target at 7 because the tests left no more. The balance pass (2026-10-06) moved The Endowment back to Tier III (now 7 / 13 / 13 / 10 / 4), revised Frontier Investment, The Waqf, Corner the Market and the shared The Grain Exchange, and changed "established commercial post" to "trading post" on The Factors' Houses and The Foreign Factor. **User pass (2026-10-07).** The user restored eight cards from Proposed cuts (The Merchant Shrines, The Assayer's Rule, The Planters' Charter, The Market Writ, The Customs Service moved to Tier III, Numidian Cavalry, The Caravanserai Network, The Exchange), added Houses of Account (Tier II), The Bourse (Tier III) and the shared Professional Soldiers, removed The Toll Roads, moved the shared Merchant Scholars to Tier III, reverted the shared The Grain Exchange to its built text, raised The Map Sellers' cap to +8, and made bought units count as trained on Bought Swords. Now 56 exclusive cards (9 / 15 / 17 / 11 / 4). **Tier 0 and Tier IV pass (2026-10-07):** added 2 Tier 0 and 11 Tier IV cards. Now 69 exclusive cards (11 / 15 / 17 / 11 / 15).

The deck's three arcs:
- **Mines and luxuries:** The Mineral Trade and Salt Tithes open; Ore Caravans and The Staple Right push toward copies; Mining Districts, Royal Assays, Strategic Exports and Corner the Market build the stockpile; The Monopoly pays it off.
- **Trade routes at home and abroad:** Provisioning Contracts, The Common Road and The Factors' Houses open; The Home Market, The League of Cities, The Foreign Factor and The Scholars' Roads shape the network; The Chartered Metropolis, The Admiralty of Trade and The Toll Roads pay for a large one; The World's Exchange turns it toward the Opus.
- **Buying instead of building:** Land Speculation opens; Private Patronage, Civic Receipts, Bought Swords and Financed Industry make purchasing the plan; Foreign Procurement, The Brokers' Redraw and The Customs Houses widen what gold buys; The Endowment, The Gilded Scaffold, The Money Lenders and A Court of Merchants lead to Merchant Princes, The Merchant Works and The Strongroom.

The Tier 0 and Tier IV pass (2026-10-07) gives each arc an opener and a late end. The Carters' Guild opens the trade-route arc before traders exist, and The Nest Egg opens the reserves direction. At Tier IV, The Spice Exchange ends the mines-and-luxuries arc beside The Monopoly; Patrons Abroad, The Trade Winds, The Embargo, The Neutral Flag and The World's Fair end the trade-route arc; Money at Work, Bought and Paid For, The Hired Garrison and The Great Loan end the buying arc; and The Merchant Dynasties pays for the great merchants called along the way.

> Your inline revisions are folded into the tables. Names for previously unnamed proposals are provisional; unspecified rarities and new cards’ tiers/rarities are editorial proposals. Existing placements, stated rarities and numerical changes are retained.

**Mining line:** Tier 0 exchanges mine/quarry production for gold. Tier I adds strategic-resource yields and mineral exports; Tier II rewards mine clusters and extra luxury copies; Tier III ends the line with The Monopoly. Private Patronage remains in Tier I, and Merchant Works remains the Tier IV project payoff. Tile yield bonuses require the tile to be worked; mine adjacency and origin-city mine counts do not require every counted mine to be worked. *(Review, 2026-10-06: The Masters' Guild, which let customs houses and manufactories join the mining economy at Tier III, is cut; the line now runs from mines to extra luxury copies to The Monopoly.)*

Eleven chairs: even a Tier IV government draws from 69 exclusive cards plus the 18 shared ones and the common pool, which is still deep enough to fill eleven chairs from two decks, and small enough that a specific pair of Commerce cards turns up in a game.

## Tier II

| Card | Rarity | Status | The card | What the game does, or why not |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Strategic Exports** | uncommon | built | Trade routes gain +1 science per improved strategic resource deposit in their origin city. Your strategic resource deposits provide twice their normal quantity. | +1 science on every trade route you send, once for every improved strategic seam inside the borders of the town it left · your strategic seams supply twice as many copies. **The second sentence touches no ground at all**, which is the user's ruling (2026-09-19): the seams on the map are what they always were, and what doubles is the total your realm holds. Three things make that exact. It is taken of the copies your **own** opened seams supply, so a copy another empire lent you is not doubled and a copy you lent away comes off the doubled figure rather than being doubled with it. It reaches strategic rows only, asked of the table's own word for a kind. And it is applied **outside** the walk that is remembered from turn to turn: that walk is kept on a clock the taking-up of a card does not move, so a law read inside it would leave every count stale for the rest of the turn — and a stale copy count is a unit a seat can or cannot build, which is how a played game starts disagreeing with a replay of its own log. Royal Assays and The Warehouses are **not** opened by this: they want a seam's own quantity and a doubling aimed at one named good, which are different questions from an empire-wide share of a total. |
| **Mining Districts** | uncommon | built | Worked mines gain +1 gold and +1 science for every two adjacent mines. | +1 gold, +1 science on every hex with a Mine, once for every two hexes with a Mine beside it. The divisor is the same field a counted line already uses, read in one more place. The neighbours need not be worked or yours; the mine being paid must be worked, as every line that lands on a hex must. Odd numbers round down. This is the first live row to use the per-neighbour reading at all. |
| **Royal Assays** | uncommon | built | Each improved luxury resource deposit with a mine provides one additional copy of that luxury. | each of your luxury deposits with a mine supplies one more copy. It went through the same door Strategic Exports opened, and the decomposition C7 built is what made it safe: the map walk is remembered on a clock a card does not move, so the walk now reports two ground facts — the copies your deposits supply, and how many of those deposits carry a mine — and the law is applied on the way out. Everything C7 established holds unchanged. No tile is written; the figure is your realm's total. It reaches the term your **own** deposits supply, so a copy lent to you is untouched and a copy you lent away comes off the raised figure. And it is luxuries only, asked of the table's own word for a kind. What is different is the arithmetic: a flat step per deposit rather than a share of a total, because "each deposit provides one additional copy" is a count and half again on three seams is not one more from each. This row had never been entered in the data at all; C8 wrote it. |
| **The Home Market** | common | built | Cities receiving at least two of your domestic routes gain +20% food, +20% production and +2 happiness, once per city. | +20% food, +20% production and +2 happiness in every city that two or more trade routes between your own cities end at. The old note was right about the gap and C5 closed it: the question a town could be asked was a yes and not a tally, and it is a tally now — how many trade routes meet this town, narrowed by which way they run and by whose town is at the far end. One walk answers it, so the yes-or-no three live cards already ask and the counts these three new ones ask cannot drift apart. The happiness is paid once per city however many carts arrive, which is the card's "once per city". The same change opened The League of Cities and The Chartered Metropolis. |
| **The Foreign Factor** | common | revised | Each foreign city holding your trading post grants you +3 gold and its host city +1 gold per turn while you are at peace and the host is not blockaded. | +3 gold a turn for every foreign city holding your trading post · +1 gold a turn in each of those cities, paid to whoever owns it. Both halves count the same houses, so the coin you take and the coin your host takes can never drift apart. The two provisos are not this card's clauses at all — they are the rule every post follows, written once where a post is read: a post pays nobody while its holder and the host are at war, or while the host city is blockaded. Nothing is lost while either holds; the house is still there when the war ends. Was: "…holding your established commercial post…". Balance pass: wording only, so the card uses one word for one thing; the effect is unchanged. |
| **The League of Cities** | rare | built | Cities with one of your paying outgoing routes gain +15% production and cost one less authority, minimum one. Cities without one lose 10% gold. | +15% production and one less authority in every city a trade route sets out from · -10% gold in every city none sets out from. **"Paying" means active** (the user's ruling, 2026-09-19): a route that has lapsed, been cancelled or been plundered is not counted, and there is no second test behind the word. Three things the old note called missing are all there now. Routes *leaving* a town are the same tally as routes arriving, asked from the other end. The mirror is the tally's own ceiling rather than a second named question — "at most none" — so the reward and its mirror name the same direction and the same kind of route, which two separate members could have drifted apart on. And what one town costs to hold is a figure a law moves; the floor works both ways, so the discount never takes a town below one and never starts charging a town that was already free. |
| **Foreign Procurement** | uncommon | built | Ignore strategic resource requirements when purchasing units. All units cost 20% more. | A unit you buy needs none of the strategic resources it would need to be built · all units cost 20% more to buy. The waiver is for the counter alone — the queue still refuses a knight with no horses — and it lifts both refusals, "you have none" and "every copy is spoken for". "All units cost 20% more" is read as the purchase price and not production, because both of the card's sentences are about the till. A piece bought this way is ordinary afterwards and still takes a copy, so an empire that buys past its iron finds the iron spoken for. The balance question the old note raised is still open. |
| **The Brokers' Redraw** | rare | built | You may reroll a draft with gold instead of faith. All other purchasing is 10% more expensive. | **Ruled: gold at a premium.** you may pay gold for a fresh hand, at a higher price than faith would ask · everything you buy costs 10% more. The redraw command carries a bank now, the way a purchase always has; the gold price is the faith ladder's own figure multiplied, so faith stays the cheaper route and the card is a convenience rather than a replacement. The multiple is a row in the statecraft sheet, not a number in the code. The ladder itself is untouched — either bank climbs the same rungs and raises the same count — and a hand whose first asking is free stays free in both. **Known gap:** nothing on screen offers the gold button yet; the rule and its price are live in the simulation, and the rail that names a bank is a UI pass. |
| **The Scholars' Roads** | rare | built | Lose 4 route capacity. Your routes gain +2 science and +2 culture, and gain +50% science and culture. | -4 trade routes · +2 science, +2 culture on every trade route you send · +50% science and culture on every trade route you send |
| **The Customs Houses** | uncommon | built | Customs houses gain +3 gold and +1 renown. Cities with a customs house gain +15% gold toward purchasing. | +3 gold on every hex with a Customs House · +1 renown a turn for every Customs House inside your borders · everything costs 15% less to buy in a town whose borders hold one. The coin wants a citizen standing on the works, as every hex line does; the renown and the discount do not. "+15% gold toward purchasing" is read as a discount of that size. |
| **The Waqf** | common | new | Faith buildings you bought with gold provide +2 faith and +1 culture. | New. Fits existing effects: The Endowment's record of which bank paid for each building, narrowed to faith buildings. Gold paid once keeps paying faith, which is the endowment the spec names for Commerce and Devotion. Was: "Purchased faith buildings provide +2 faith and +1 culture." Balance pass: read from every bank, it stacked on The Offered Stones and The Endowment for faith-bought buildings; gold paid once becoming faith is the endowment idea. |

Probably fits existing effects: trade routes already carry religious pressure as a rules figure, and a route line can already ask about the city it reaches. Check that a card may move that figure. Merchant missionaries, for Commerce and Devotion. |

The card then leaves its chair. | New. Needs: commissions, and a count of copies of one named luxury, including copies received in deals (the same per-luxury count The Monopoly reads). ## Tier III

| Card | Rarity | Status | The card | What the game does, or why not |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Caravanserai Cities** | uncommon | built | Caravanserais can be built in every city. Cities with a Caravanserai gain +20% gold. | you may build a Caravanserai in every city · +20% gold in every city holding one. **Ruled: a caravanserai stays an empire building** (the user, 2026-09-19: *"we need two different flags, can be built once and is empire building"*). So the mark that limited the house and the mark that classed it are two marks now, and every building that carried the old one carries both — nothing about any existing row moved. The card lifts the **limit** and leaves the **class** exactly where it was, which is the whole of why it is coherent: a realm may raise a yard in every town, and every one of them is still priced against how many towns it will serve, still admitted wherever a card asks for a town holding one of the realm's great houses, still counted as one of them, and still passed over by a discount written for the ordinary shelves. The card buys many of an expensive thing rather than turning it into a cheap one. One thing had to be made safe alongside it: the walk that gathers what a realm's great houses do used to read each town's shelf in turn, which was harmless while a realm could hold only one of each, so it now reads each row **once** however many copies stand — otherwise the yard's own gift to every caravan leaving that town would have been paid once per yard. This row had never been entered in the data at all; C4 entered it deferred and C7 lit it. |
| **A Court of Merchants** | rare | built | Gain +50% renown, but great-person offers contain only Great Merchants. | **Ruled: fall back to the normal draw.** +50% renown a turn · every great-person offer shows only great merchants, until there are none left to call. The share is taken of the whole recurring trickle and never of a triumph's lump. The narrowing is a strong nudge and not a lock: when every great merchant in the world has been called, the draft goes back to the whole roster, so the standing rule that a spent roster banks rather than blocks survives. A draft somebody bought narrowed to another family — the Academy's scholars — is dealt as what it was bought as. This row had never been entered in the data at all; C3 wrote it. |
| **The Money Lenders** | rare | built | Earn interest equal to 2% of your treasury each turn, with no cap. | +1 gold per 50 gold in the treasury — a coin for every fiftieth, which is the two per hundred the card quotes, floored once. The old ceiling and the purchasing surcharge are both gone with the revision. |
| **The Chartered Metropolis** | rare | built | Cities with at least three of your paying outgoing routes gain +25% food, production and culture, but each costs +4 authority while qualified. | +25% food, +25% production and +25% culture in every city three or more trade routes set out from · +4 authority for each such city. All three of the old note's gaps closed together in C5. **"Paying" means active** (the user's ruling, 2026-09-19) — a lapsed, cancelled or plundered route is not counted, and nothing else is tested. "While qualified" falls out of the shape rather than needing a clause: the surcharge is a scoped repricing asked fresh every turn, so a city that drops to two routes stops paying it that turn. |
| **The Admiralty of Trade** | rare | revised | A sea trade route between two cities that both hold your trading post has no range limit. | **Revised in the 2026-10-06 review (wording only; the effect is unchanged).** Was: "Your sea routes may connect two cities holding your established commercial posts regardless of range. A legal sea path, access, peace and route capacity are still required." a sea trade route between two towns that both hold your trading post may be sent any distance. One named rule read at the one place the gate prices a route's reach, beside the clause it lifts — the shape three other live cards in this deck use for a refusal. It is narrow on purpose. The route must run **by sea**; both towns must hold a post of yours that is actually **paying**, so a war or a blockade suspends the privilege exactly as it suspends a post's income (the design says "card range privileges" in those words, so this is the rule every post follows rather than a clause of this card's); and one post is not two. The card's second sentence is then true by construction rather than by a second reading: every other clause of the gate still runs, so a sea lane no caravan could sail, a partner you have not met, a war, a full slot table and a trade route already running that way are all still refused. |
| **The Gilded Scaffold** | rare | built | You may purchase world wonders. All your cities lose 15% production. | **Ruled: build it as written.** you may buy world wonders with gold · -15% production in every city. The lift is a second clause on the one `if` that refuses a wonder at the counter, beside the faith lift the Valley of Kings already had — not a second way to buy one — so every gate below it is asked unchanged: a wonder another empire has claimed, one whose technology is not in, and one whose site the ground does not hold are all still refused. The price is the row's full cost in hammers at the ordinary gold rate. What the refusal protected is now paid for by the card's other half rather than by the rule. |
| **The Endowment** | uncommon | revised | Purchased buildings provide +1 science each, at most +3 per town. | +2 science in every city per purchased building there. C4's measurement was exact and the missing piece was the only one: a town now records **which bank paid for each of its roofs**, beside the turn they went up, written by the one seam that puts stones in a town and by nothing else (schema 123). It replaces nothing — the ledger of firsts still marks a town's first purchase, and still cannot say which roof it was — because the two answer different questions. Either bank counts: a library bought with faith is as bought as one bought with gold, which is what the word "purchased" says. A roof completed in the yard, granted by a card, raised as a founding Monument or laid as a relic records nothing, and absence is the shape every town saved before the field already had. A captured town brings the record with it, so a conqueror is paid for the roofs its last owner bought — pay follows the stones, as everywhere else. **The sheet's text is the one built**; the data row had drifted to a much larger sentence about a quarter of every native yield, and that is gone. Was: Tier II, common, "Purchased buildings provide +2 science." Balance pass: uncapped science per bought building, in the deck that buys everything; it goes back to Tier III and uncommon, where the data has it, with a ceiling of +3 per town. |
| **A Guild Commission *(commission)*** | uncommon | new | Commission. Goal: buy five buildings with gold while seated. Reward: a free great-person draft, the same offer Merchant Princes sells for gold. The card then leaves its chair. | New. Needs: commissions. The reward is an offer the game already prices. For Commerce and Magisterial. |
| **The Monopoly** | rare | new | For each luxury you hold three or more copies of and no other empire holds, gain +5 gold, +3 culture and +1 happiness in every city. | New. Needs: a reading of whether any other empire holds a given luxury. Counts of your own copies exist; nothing asks about other empires' copies of one good. Monopolies are a spec theme no other card covers. |
| **The Customs Service** | uncommon | new | Trade routes leaving a city whose borders hold a customs house gain +2 gold and +2 culture. | Restored by the user (2026-10-07) from Proposed cuts and moved from Tier I to Tier III, where a great merchant's customs house is likely to be standing. Fits existing effects: a route line narrowed by a work inside the origin's borders. |
| **The Bourse** | rare | new | Gold buildings produce 50% more of their own yields. | Added by the user (2026-10-07). Needs: a percentage on a building's own yield lines. Read as the buildings' base yields only, so it does not multiply card bonuses paid per gold building (Commercial Education, Houses of Account). |

A rival racing for the Opus either sends or accepts a trade route, which pays you, or builds slower. It is a penalty on a rival, not a bonus toward your own Opus, so the pending +60% cap does not apply to it either way. The bots would need to weigh opening a trade route to the holder. |

Reward: +50% science and +50% culture in every city for ten turns. The card then leaves its chair. | New. Big moment. Needs: commissions. The reward is a timed effect with an absolute end turn, the shape timed effects already take. Rewritten for ruling (qqqqqq) 6, 2026-10-12. Was: "Goal: have trade routes running to three different foreign empires at the same time, or to every foreign empire still standing if fewer than three remain." A foreign trade route needs peace with its host, so a rival at war with the seat could keep the goal out of reach. Domestic trade routes are always the seat's own to send, so the goal now asks only for a large network, which is the deck's late trade-route arc at full size. |
| **The Great Loan** | rare | new | When you seat this card, gain gold equal to twenty turns of your gold income. For the next forty turns your cities lose 25% gold. Borrowing against a future the game may not reach: a seat near the end spends twenty turns of gold at once on Merchant Princes, The Gilded Scaffold or the Opus itself, which takes gold. Repaying costs ten turns of gold if the game runs that long. With The Strongroom on the shelf, the pending cap on its reward (review summary item 17) matters more. |
| **The Trade Winds** | rare | new | Gain +3 trade route capacity. Your trade routes reach 50% farther. | New. Late signature. Probably fits existing effects: trade route capacity is already a card line (The Scholars' Roads takes four away), and a trade route's reach is a rules figure a card can raise by a percentage, the shape Venture Routes uses for the term. Check that the reach, not only the term, is open to a card. The deck's trade routes at their widest, for the last ages. |

## Synergies with other decks

Each pair below follows the matching entry in `docs/decks/deck-design.md` ("What pairs of decks should enable"). A **hook** is something one deck's cards create that the other deck's cards read. This sheet creates its hooks whether or not the partner is seated. Only cards that survive the 2026-10-06 review are named.

### Commerce and Dominion: merchants and their guards
- **Commerce gives Dominion** purchases. Gold buys the buildings an army has no production to spare for, and buys units in an emergency.
- **Commerce gets back** protected trade routes, plunder turned into gold, and reparations from defeated empires.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** a gold reserve (The Money Lenders, The Strongroom, Money at Work, and the shared War Bonds, which turns it into strength), trade routes that need guarding (every trade route the deck sends; the shared The Escorted Roads pays for the guard), and units bought with gold (Bought Swords, Foreign Procurement, and the shared Mercenary Contracts and The Chartered Company).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** gold from plunder and kills fills the treasury that The Money Lenders and The Strongroom read.
- **Shared improvements:** mines on strategic resources. Commerce takes gold and science from them (The Mineral Trade, Strategic Exports, Ore Caravans); Dominion builds its army on them.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** Bought Swords, Foreign Procurement, The Hired Garrison (units bought with gold to hold a wonder or Opus city), and the shared The Escorted Roads, Letters of Marque, War Bonds (strength paid for with gold), Mercenary Contracts (hired armies) and The Chartered Company (a charter for a unit bought only with gold).
- **Not carded here:** tribute is closer to Dominion's mechanic and already exists as a deal term. Naval raiding paid in gold is the shared Letters of Marque.

### Commerce and Expansionist: the land and the market
- **Commerce gives Expansionist** purchases: gold buys tiles, workers and settlers, so the empire grows faster than food alone allows.
- **Commerce gets back** goods to sell (claimed land opens resources) and surplus food to carry on trade routes.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** gold, and trade routes that carry food (Provisioning Contracts, The Home Market, the shared The Grain Exchange and Market Gardens).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** opened resources (Salt Tithes, Ore Caravans, Royal Assays, The Staple Right, The Spice Exchange) and worked mines (Mining Districts).
- **Shared improvements:** mines and quarries. Expansionist works them for production; Commerce sells what they produce.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** Land Speculation, Frontier Investment (bringing small towns up to strength), Provisioning Contracts, The Home Market (market towns where several trade routes meet), The League of Cities, and the shared Market Gardens, The Grain Exchange (the grain supply) and The Provincial Fair.
- **Not carded here:** canals would be a new improvement, a larger decision than a card. Tiles a trade route passes through growing richer (The Waystations) is proposed for cut; the path reading it needed stays alive through The Toll Roads.

### Commerce and Devotion: pilgrims and markets
- **Commerce gives Devotion** trade routes that carry religion, so faith spreads along them.
- **Commerce gets back** pilgrims: holy sites as destinations, and faith paid on trade routes.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** trade routes, religious pressure carried on them (The Silk Road Monks), and buildings bought with gold (the record The Endowment and The Waqf read).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** holy sites (Pilgrim Markets) and cities following your religion (The Silk Road Monks).
- **Shared improvements:** plantations. Commerce takes gold and food from them (Coastal Estates); Devotion takes faith.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Waqf (endowments), The Silk Road Monks (merchant missionaries), and the shared Pilgrim Markets (pilgrim roads) and The Tithe.
- **Gap:** neither deck covers the other's production. The pair buys with gold and with faith and builds almost nothing; the spec names it as the first pair to check in playtesting.

### Commerce and Scientific: the patrons
- **Commerce gives Scientific** gold that buys libraries and universities, and foreign trade routes that pay science.
- **Commerce gets back** technologies that open trade earlier: more trade routes, earlier ships, earlier trade buildings.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** gold, foreign trade routes, and buildings bought with gold (The Endowment pays science on each).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** any trade unlock that arrives early, such as Scientific's extra trade route from Printing, is used at once by Venture Routes and The Scholars' Roads.
- **Shared improvements:** mines, quarries and plantations. Commerce pays gold on them; Scientific pays science (the shared The Exchange of Discoveries already does).
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** Commercial Education, Strategic Exports, The Scholars' Roads, The Endowment, and the shared Merchant Scholars, The Merchant Navigators, The Exchange of Discoveries and Books from the Ships (books from the ships).
- **Exploration:** the spec gives exploration to Commerce and asks that it be light on Scientific's sheet. The Pathfinders' Company, The Map Sellers and Travellers' Letters are this deck's exploration cards; all three sit at Tier 0 and lead into foreign trade routes.

### Commerce and Magisterial: the art market
- **Commerce gives Magisterial** gold that buys rerolls and drafts, and great merchants and customs houses for its any-family cards.
- **Commerce gets back** culture turned into gold, and boons that save purchases.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** gold, a gold price on a redraw (The Brokers' Redraw) and on a great-person draft (Merchant Princes), and customs houses (The Customs Houses).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** cards drafted (the shared The Art Dealers), great-person works on trade routes (the shared The Cosmopolitan Court) and the count of decks seated in your government (the shared Travelling Players, as revised on this sheet).
- **Shared improvements:** customs houses, and landmarks on trade routes.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Brokers' Redraw, Merchant Princes, A Court of Merchants, The Customs Houses, The Merchant Dynasties (customs houses paying culture), A Guild Commission (guild commissions), and the shared The Art Dealers (gold for every card drafted, the pair's Tier I card), Travelling Players and The Cosmopolitan Court.

The full notes of each row are in git (commit a462c76). Rows with Pass `reconcile` were cut when the six sheets were reconciled, because a twin on another sheet became the shared card.

## Shared cards for the user to rule on

Only one of the two sheets recommends a change to these, so each stays on both shelves until the user rules.
- **Market Gardens** (with Expansionist): Commerce recommends cutting it, because it is filler for Commerce and its trade-route food repeats Provisioning Contracts. Expansionist does not comment.
- **The Provincial Fair** (with Expansionist): Commerce recommends cutting it, because it stacks three conditions (connected, not the capital, a Market) for flat yields and changes no decision. Expansionist does not comment.
- **Merchant Scholars** (with Scientific): Scientific recommends keeping it but narrowing it to count Academies rather than every family's works, since Scientific's great-person cards read Academies only. Commerce does not comment.
